text: Which layer of the TCP/IP Protocol Suite does the IP (Internet Protocol) belong to?
info: IP, ICMP, IGMP, ARP, and RARP operate at the Network layer to handle addressing and routing across networks.

text: Which Transport Layer protocol focuses on connection-oriented transmission and guarantees data delivery?
info: TCP = Connection-oriented (Reliable/Guaranteed delivery); UDP = Connectionless (Fast/Best-effort).

text: Which of the following is NOT a main characteristic of the IP protocol?
info: The three main characteristics of IP are Unreliable, Connectionless, and Best-effort delivery.

text: What is the name of the data packet at the IP Layer?
info: Data Link = Frame, Transport = Segment/User Datagram, IP = Datagram.

text: If an IP Datagram has no Options added, what is the fixed size of the Header?
info: The base IP Header without Options is always 20 Bytes.

text: What is the maximum possible size of an IP Header when Options are included?
info: IP Header size ranges from 20 to 60 Bytes (Base 20 + Max Options 40).

text: The Total Size of an IP Datagram ranges between how many bytes?
info: Total Size ranges from 20 to 65,535 Bytes (based on the 16-bit Total Length field: 2^16 - 1).

text: Which field in the IP Header prevents a packet from circulating infinitely in the network?
info: TTL sets the maximum lifespan/hop count to prevent routing loops.

text: How many bits are allocated for the Source IP address and Destination IP address fields in an IPv4 Header?
info: IPv4 addresses are 32 bits (4 Bytes) for both Source and Destination.

text: What is the unit of measurement for the HLEN (Header Length) field?
info: HLEN measures in 4-byte increments (Actual Header Bytes = HLEN × 4).

text: If there are no Options, what binary value is set in the HLEN field of the IP Header?
info: Header 20 Bytes / 4 = 5. In 4-bit binary, 5 is 0101.

text: In the original Service Type (TOS) format, what was the purpose of the Precedence subfield (first 3 bits), and what is its status in IPv4?
info: The Precedence subfield was designed for priority but is not utilized in IPv4.

answers.text: Define priority level / Not used in IPv4

text: Setting the TOS Bits to 1000 corresponds to which service type?
info: 1000 = Minimize delay, 0100 = Maximize throughput, 0010 = Maximize reliability, 0001 = Minimize cost.

text: Which TOS Bits setting should be used for applications like TELNET, Interactive activities, and DNS (UDP query)?
info: Real-time/interactive services require low latency -> Minimize delay.

text: In Differentiated Services (DiffServ), how many bits long is the Codepoint (DSCP) field?
info: DiffServ uses the first 6 bits for DSCP and reserves the remaining 2 bits for ECN.

text: Codepoint values ending in XXXX11 (Category 2) are assigned for use by which authority/scope?
info: XXXXX0 = IETF, XXXX11 = Local, XXXX01 = Temporary/Experimental.

text: What is the correct formula to calculate the actual Data Size in an IP Datagram?
info: Total Length = Header + Data, so Data = Total Length - Header Length.

answers.text: Data Size = Header Length + Total Length
Data Size = Total Length - Header Length

text: Why must Padding be added to an Ethernet Frame when sending a small IP Datagram?
info: Ethernet minimum payload is 46 Bytes. Smaller IP datagrams require padding.

answers.text: Because IP Header requires a fixed 60 Bytes length
Because Ethernet Frame enforces a minimum Payload size of at least 46 Bytes

text: If the first 8 bits of an IP Packet are 01000010, how will the receiver handle it and why?
info: The last 4 bits 0010 = 2 (2 × 4 = 8 Bytes). Invalid IPv4 header size (<20 Bytes), so it must be discarded.

answers.text: Accept the packet because the header is 20 Bytes
Discard the packet because HLEN equals 2 (2 × 4 = 8 Bytes), which is below the minimum 20 Bytes
Forward the packet because it is a valid IPv4
Fragment the packet because it exceeds standard size

text: If the HLEN in an IP Packet is 1000 in binary, how many Bytes of Options are present?
info: 1000_2 = 8 -> Total Header = 8 × 4 = 32 Bytes. Options = 32 - 20 = 12 Bytes.

text: A Protocol field value of 6 in the IP Header represents which higher-layer protocol?
info: 1 = ICMP, 2 = IGMP, 6 = TCP, 17 = UDP, 89 = OSPF.

text: A Protocol field value of 17 in the IP Header represents which higher-layer protocol?
info: 17 = UDP, 6 = TCP.

text: What is the process called when the receiving Network Layer reads the Protocol field to deliver the packet to the correct target protocol?
info: Demultiplexing inspects the Protocol field to dispatch data upward to the correct transport protocol.

text: How do the Source Address and Destination Address fields change while traveling through routers in the network?
info: Original Source and Destination IP addresses remain intact end-to-end.

answers.text: Do not change at all throughout the journey

text: What is the Maximum Transmission Unit (MTU) of a standard Ethernet network in bytes?
info: Standard Ethernet MTU = 1,500 Bytes.

text: Why is the Fragmentation process necessary?
info: If IP Datagram Size > Link MTU, it must be fragmented to fit through the physical link.

answers.text: Because the IP Datagram size is larger than the MTU of the next link
To securely change the Source IP Address
To force packets through TCP only

text: Which device in the network is responsible for Reassembly (combining fragments back into the original datagram)?
info: Routers can fragment datagrams, but only the Destination Host performs reassembly.

text: Which 16-bit field in the IP Header identifies fragments belonging to the exact same original IP Datagram?
info: All fragments from the same original packet share the same Identification number.

text: Which field in the IP Header can be inspected to see how many more hops a packet can travel before being dropped?
info: TTL decrements by 1 at each router hop. When TTL reaches 0, the packet is discarded.

text: When an IP Datagram undergoes Fragmentation, which field in the IP Header does NOT change its value?
info: Identification and IP addresses are copied unchanged to all fragments.

text: What is the size of the Flags field in the IP Header, and what is the purpose of the 1st bit?
info: Flags field has 3 bits: 1st bit = Reserved (0), 2nd bit = DF, 3rd bit = MF.

text: If the Do Not Fragment (DF bit) is set to 1 and the packet size exceeds the next link's MTU, what will the router do?
info: DF = 1 forbids fragmentation. If it cannot pass, the router must drop it and report via ICMP.

answers.text: Discard the packet and send an ICMP Error Message back to the source
Ignore the MTU limit and forward the packet
Record the data in the Options field

text: What does a More Fragments (MF bit) value of 1 indicate?
info: MF = 1 means more fragments follow; MF = 0 means it is either the last fragment or non-fragmented.

answers.text: This is NOT the last fragment (more fragments follow)
An error occurred in this packet

text: The Fragmentation Offset field is 13 bits long. What unit does it use to measure data positioning?
info: Offset is measured in 8-byte blocks (Offset = Start Byte / 8).

text: What is the Offset value of the First Fragment in a fragmentation sequence?
info: The first fragment starts at byte 0, so Offset = 0 / 8 = 0.

text: If a packet has MF = 0 and Offset = 0, what is its fragmentation status?
info: MF = 0 (no more fragments) + Offset = 0 (starts at 0) = Standalone, unfragmented packet.

answers.text: Last fragment of a large packet

text: If a packet has MF = 1 and Offset = 0, what is its fragmentation status?
info: Offset = 0 indicates it is the start; MF = 1 indicates more fragments follow -> First fragment.

text: If a packet has a Fragmentation Offset of 100, what is the First Byte Number of the payload in this packet?
info: First Byte = Offset × 8 = 100 × 8 = 800.

text: Given: Offset = 100, HLEN = 5, Total Length = 100. Find the Last Byte Number of the data in this fragment.
info: First Byte = 100 × 8 = 800, Header Size = 5 × 4 = 20 Bytes, Data Size = 100 - 20 = 80 Bytes, Last Byte = First Byte + Data Size - 1 = 800 + 80 - 1 = 879.

text: If an IP Datagram is fragmented into 3 Fragments, which fragment(s) will have an MF bit value of 0?
info: Fragments 1 and 2 have MF = 1, while only the last fragment (3) has MF = 0.

text: Into how many main categories are IP Options divided based on option size?
info: IP Options are grouped into 1-byte options (Single-byte) and multi-byte options (Multiple-byte).

text: Which options belong entirely to the Single-byte Options group?
info: Single-byte Options consist of only two types: No Operation (NOP) and End of Option (EOP).

answers.text: No operation and End of option
Strict source route and Loose source route

text: What does the first bit (Copy bit) in the Option Code field control?
info: Copy bit = 0 (keep in 1st fragment only), Copy bit = 1 (copy to all fragments).

answers.text: Controls whether the option is copied to all fragments during fragmentation

text: Which options will be copied to all fragments during fragmentation (Copy bit = 1)?
info: Only Strict Source Route (Code 137) and Loose Source Route (Code 131) have Copy bit = 1.

answers.text: No operation and End of option
Strict source route and Loose source route
Record route and Strict source route

text: Which option acts as filler to align the start of the next option on a 32-bit boundary?
info: No Operation (NOP) is used for padding and memory alignment.

text: Which statement is correct regarding End of Option (EOP)?
info: End of Option (Code 0) marks the end of options area and can only appear once at the very end.

answers.text: Can be placed anywhere inside the Options field
Multiple End of Options can be included in the same packet
Placed only at the end of the Options field, limited to exactly 1 instance
Always has a fixed length of 4 Bytes

text: What is the maximum number of router IP addresses that the Record Route Option can record, and why?
info: Maximum Options space is 40 Bytes, allowing a maximum of 9 recorded IPv4 addresses.

answers.text: 9 routers / Limited by max 40 Bytes Options field (9 × 4 = 36 Bytes + 4 Bytes Option Header)

text: What is the function of the Pointer field in the Record Route Option, and what is its initial value?
info: Pointer starts at offset 4 (first slot) and increments by 4 after each IP is recorded.

answers.text: Points to source router / Initial value = 0
Points to the first available slot to record an IP / Initial value = 4
Points to fragment index / Initial value = 1
Points to end of packet / Initial value = 20

text: What is the strictest rule of the Strict Source Route Option?
info: Strict Source Route enforces exact path adherence; hitting an unlisted router causes immediate packet drop.

answers.text: Records only incoming router IP addresses
The packet MUST visit every router listed and CANNOT pass through any unlisted routers
Allowed to bypass routers if network congestion occurs
Operates only when Transport Layer is UDP

text: Which option correctly describes the difference between Strict Source Route and Loose Source Route?
info: Strict = Exact path matching; Loose = Flexible path allowing extra intermediate routers.

answers.text: Strict records timestamps, Loose does not
Strict forbids taking unlisted hops, whereas Loose allows visiting unlisted routers along the path
Strict is 1 Byte, Loose is multi-byte
Strict operates at Transport Layer, Loose at Network Layer

text: In what unit is time recorded in the Timestamp Option, and from when is it counted?
info: Timestamp measures milliseconds elapsed since Midnight Universal Time (UTC).

text: Setting Flag = 1 in the Timestamp Option causes the router to record data in which format?
info: Flag 0 = Time only, Flag 1 = IP + Time, Flag 3 = Pre-specified IP + Time.

answers.text: Records paired Outgoing IP address + Timestamp

text: What is the purpose of the 4-bit Overflow (O-Flow) field in the Timestamp Option?
info: Overflow counts how many routers could not record timestamps due to lack of space.

answers.text: Records the number of routers skipped because option space became full

text: If a router finds that the Record Route Option space is full, how will it handle the packet?
info: When Record Route space is full, the router simply stops recording and forwards normally.

answers.text: Forward the packet without recording additional IP addresses
Send ICMP Error reporting Option Overflow
Fragment the packet to expand Options space

text: Which field in the IP Header is primarily utilized by diagnostic tools (like Traceroute) to measure distance and trace paths hop-by-hop?
info: Path tracing tools send packets with TTL = 1, 2, 3... to trigger TTL expiration at each hop.

text: In which IP Header Option does the sender place intermediate router IP addresses in the Option field while placing the current target hop into the Destination IP field?
info: Source Routing swaps Destination IP addresses dynamically as the packet moves through designated routers.

answers.text: Source Route Option (both Strict and Loose)

text: What mathematical system is used to calculate the IP Header Checksum at the Sender side?
info: IP Checksum uses One's complement addition across all header words, followed by bit inversion.

text: During the sender's Checksum creation step, what is the initial value set for the Header Checksum field prior to calculation?
info: The Checksum field itself must be set to 0000 0000 0000 0000 (All 0s) before computing.

text: When the receiver processes the packet and sums all header fields including the Checksum, what complement result accepts the packet as valid?
info: At the receiver, summing all header fields (including checksum) and taking one's complement must yield 0 to be accepted.

text: What portion of the IP Datagram is protected by the Header Checksum field?
info: IP Header Checksum validates only the IP Header. Payload integrity is handled by higher-layer protocols (TCP/UDP).
